content: The document outlines strategies for monitoring and improving the quality of care for maternal infections, specifically during the peripartum period. These recommendations are designed to guide the development of clinical protocols and health policies, rather than serving as a comprehensive manual for the prevention and management of maternal infections. Target Audience The intended audience includes healthcare professionals responsible for creating national and local health protocols and policies, as well as managers of maternal and child health programs and public health policymakers in all settings. For policymakers, the guideline provides evidence-based justification to support the formulation of relevant policies and resource allocation, particularly in regions where maternal and newborn deaths due to peripartum infections are significant. Additionally, the guideline is useful for obstetricians, midwives, nurses, and general practitioners directly involved in the care of pregnant women. In areas with limited healthcare workforce, where task-shifting is necessary, the guideline can assist mid-level providers in selecting appropriate interventions to prevent or treat maternal infections before referring patients to higher levels of care. Scope of the Guideline The guideline focuses on pregnant women or those who have recently given birth and are at risk of, or diagnosed with, bacterial infections of the genital tract or surrounding tissues during or after vaginal or cesarean delivery. It also considers the impact of these infections on their fetus or newborn. However, infections caused by viral, fungal, or other infectious agents, as well as bacterial infections in areas outside the genital tract, are excluded from the scope. Background and Methods The guideline represents the World Health Organization’s (WHO) commitment to evidence-based policies and practices. It was developed using standard operating procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process included identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. Contributors to the Guideline 1. WHO Steering Group: This group, composed of WHO staff from the Departments of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) and Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA), managed the entire guideline development process. They drafted the scope, formulated key questions, identified systematic review teams, and supervised evidence synthesis and retrieval. They also organized the guideline panel meeting, finalized the document, and managed its dissemination and evaluation. 2. Guideline Development Group (GDG): This group included 15 external experts and stakeholders from all six WHO regions, ensuring geographic and gender representation. Members were selected for their expertise in research, guideline development, clinical policy, and maternal infection management. Representatives of women affected by the recommendations were also included. The GDG reviewed evidence, interpreted findings, and formulated final recommendations. 3. External Review Group: This group consisted of six technical experts and stakeholders who reviewed the final guideline document for factual accuracy, clarity, and contextual relevance. 4. Systematic Review Team and Methodologists: Evidence was primarily sourced from Cochrane systematic reviews maintained by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group. Where necessary, non-Cochrane reviews were conducted by technical staff from the Department of Health Policy at the National Center for Child Health and Development (NCCHD) in Japan. The evidence was appraised using the GRADE methodology to assess its quality and relevance. 5. External Partners and Observers: Representatives from organizations such as FIGO, ICM, UNFPA, USAID, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, and NICE participated as observers during the final guideline development meeting. These organizations are potential implementers of the guideline and have a history of collaboration with WHO. Evidence Retrieval and Assessment The systematic review team retrieved evidence from Cochrane reviews of randomized controlled trials and non-randomized studies. Reviews were updated if they were more than two years old. In cases where no suitable reviews existed, new systematic reviews were conducted. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, which considers factors such as study design limitations, inconsistency of results, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Formulation of Recommendations The GRADE framework was used to draft recommendations based on synthesized evidence. The WHO Steering Group considered the quality of evidence, balance of benefits and risks, values and preferences, and resource implications. Recommendations were categorized as “strong” or “conditional” based on the quality of evidence and other factors. Evidence-to-decision tables documented the rationale for each recommendation. Declaration of Interests All external contributors were required to declare potential conflicts of interest before participating in the guideline development process. The WHO Steering Group reviewed these declarations to determine their impact on the contributors’ objectivity. Experts with significant conflicts were restricted from participating in discussions or formulating recommendations related to their conflicts. Decision-Making Process During the technical consultation, participants discussed and revised draft recommendations. Final adoption of recommendations was achieved through consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of participants. In cases of unresolved disputes, decisions were made by majority vote. Observers and WHO staff were not eligible to vote. Document Preparation and Peer Review The WHO Steering Group prepared a draft guideline document, which was reviewed by GDG members and the External Review Group.
